name: AARM Funnel
description: A metrics framework for reasoning about a product's user lifecycle, useful for "how would you improve metric X" or "diagnose this funnel" questions.
example: Prompt: "DAU for our app dropped 15% last month — how do you investigate?" Use the funnel to isolate which stage regressed before hypothesizing why.
steps: Acquisition — how new users find and first arrive at the product.
Activation — whether a new user reaches a meaningful first-value moment.
Retention — whether users come back and keep using the product over time.
Monetization — whether and how the product converts usage into revenue.
For a metric-drop question: identify which stage moved first, then hypothesize causes specific to that stage rather than the whole funnel at once.

name: CIRCLES
description: A structured approach to product design questions ("design a product for X") that makes sure you cover the problem space before jumping to solutions.
example: Prompt: "Design an alarm clock for the visually impaired." Walk through each step below out loud, spending the most time on Identify and List.
steps: Comprehend the situation — clarify the user, the goal, and any constraints before proposing anything.
Identify the customer — pick a specific user segment to design for, not "everyone".
Report the customer's needs — list what that segment actually needs, in their words.
Cut, through prioritization — pick the 1-2 needs worth solving first and say why.
List solutions — brainstorm multiple ways to address the prioritized need(s).
Evaluate trade-offs — weigh the solutions against impact, effort, and constraints.
Summarize your recommendation — state your pick and the reasoning in one or two sentences.

name: HEART Framework (Google)
description: Google's user-centered UX and product metrics framework evaluating Happiness, Engagement, Adoption, Retention, and Task Success through Goals-Signals-Metrics.
example: Redesigning checkout flow: Goal = Task Success. Signal = Users checkout without errors. Metric = Checkout completion rate and average time-to-checkout.
steps: Happiness: User satisfaction, Net Promoter Score (NPS), perceived ease of use, sentiment ratings.
Engagement: Frequency, depth, and intensity of interaction (e.g. daily active visits, comments per user, session duration).
Adoption: How many new users start using a product or newly launched feature within a given timeframe.
Retention: Percentage of users returning over time (cohort retention at Day 1, Day 7, Day 30, churn rate).
Task Success: Efficiency and effectiveness of key user workflows (error rate, time to complete task, task completion rate).
For each category, define: (1) Goal (what user need are we solving?), (2) Signal (what user behavior indicates success?), (3) Metric (what quantitative KPI do we track?).
when_to_use: Use when defining north-star metrics and telemetry for a specific feature, UX redesign, or consumer app.
when_not_to_use: Do not try to track all 5 dimensions equally on every project; pick the 1-2 most critical to the current phase.
pitfalls: Tracking vanity engagement metrics (pageviews) without measuring task success or user satisfaction.
Failing to tie signals to measurable KPIs.

name: ICE Score
description: A faster, rougher cousin of RICE for prioritization under time pressure - three factors instead of four, each scored 1-10.
example: Prompt: "Here are 8 backlog items, rank them in 2 minutes." ICE is fast enough to actually do live, where RICE's reach math often is not.
steps: Impact — how much this moves the goal metric if it works, 1-10.
Confidence — how sure you are the impact estimate is right, 1-10.
Ease — how cheap/fast this is to ship, 1-10 (inverse of effort).
Score = (Impact + Confidence + Ease) / 3, or just add them - rank by score, then sanity-check the top 2-3 against judgment out loud.
when_to_use: Use it when you need to rank a long list quickly (10+ ideas) or the prompt explicitly wants speed over precision.
when_not_to_use: Prefer RICE when the interviewer wants to see you reason about reach explicitly, or when effort estimates matter more than a quick gut-check.
pitfalls: Scoring everything a 7-8 out of politeness, which flattens the ranking and defeats the point.
Not stating what "10" and "1" anchor to before scoring, so the numbers are not comparable across ideas.

name: Jobs To Be Done
description: Reframes "who is the user" questions around what job the customer is really "hiring" the product to do, independent of any specific solution.
example: Prompt: "Why do people buy a $5 milkshake in the morning?" The classic JTBD answer: commuters are "hiring" it for a long, one-handed, filling companion for a boring drive - not because they wanted a dessert.
steps: State the job in the customer's words: "When [situation], I want to [motivation], so I can [outcome]."
Separate the functional job (the practical task) from the emotional and social jobs (how they want to feel, how they want to be seen).
Identify who/what the product is really competing with - often not the obvious category competitor, but whatever else currently gets the job done.
Design the solution around making that job easier, faster, or more reliable - not around adding features nobody hired the product to do.
when_to_use: Use it when a prompt asks you to design for an underserved need, explain why customers switch products, or find whitegespace competitors are missing.
when_not_to_use: Skip it for pure prioritization or metrics questions - JTBD explains motivation, it does not rank options or diagnose a funnel.
pitfalls: Stating the job as a feature ("wants a faster checkout") instead of the underlying goal ("wants to feel confident the purchase went through").
Forgetting the functional/emotional/social dimensions of a job - most real jobs have all three.

name: Kano Model
description: Classifies customer preferences and product features into five emotional categories to guide roadmaps and balance basic expectations against delight.
example: Ride-hailing app: Must-have = Getting picked up and dropped off safely. Performance = Pickup wait time under 3 minutes. Delighter = Free in-car water and preferred Spotify playlist connected.
steps: Must-Have / Basic Needs: Taken for granted when present, causes extreme dissatisfaction when absent (e.g. mobile app login, braking in a car).
Performance / Linear Needs: Customer satisfaction increases proportionally with execution (e.g. battery life, search speed, storage capacity).
Delighters / Attractive Needs: Unexpected features that create high customer joy when present, but cause zero dissatisfaction when omitted (e.g. free flight upgrade, AI auto-summaries).
Indifferent Features: Customers do not care either way — eliminate to save engineering bandwidth.
Reverse Features: Features that actively annoy users when present (e.g. auto-playing sound, intrusive popups).
Natural Decay: Note that yesterday's Delighter becomes today's Performance feature and tomorrow's Must-Have.
when_to_use: Use when prioritizing a roadmap to ensure basic reliability isn't sacrificed for flashy features.
when_not_to_use: Do not use without direct user research; assumptions about what constitutes a 'delighter' are frequently wrong.
pitfalls: Investing heavily in delighters while the core must-have features are buggy or unreliable.
Forgetting that customer expectations rise over time, shifting features downward.

name: North Star Metric
description: The single metric that best captures the core value a product delivers to customers - used to align a team around one number instead of a dashboard of vanity metrics.
example: Spotify's North Star is closer to "time spent listening" than "subscription revenue" - revenue follows if that number is healthy.
steps: Identify the core value exchange: what does the customer actually get, and when do they get it?
Pick a metric that only moves when real value is delivered (not a proxy that can be gamed).
Check it is leading, not lagging - it should predict revenue/retention, not just restate them.
Break it into 2-4 input metrics your team can actually influence day to day.
when_to_use: Use it for "how would you measure success for this product" or "what metric would you track" questions.
when_not_to_use: Do not use it as a stand-in for a full metrics tree - a North Star is one number for alignment, not a diagnostic tool for "why did this metric move".
pitfalls: Picking a metric that is easy to move but does not track real value (e.g. app opens instead of completed trips).
Picking a pure revenue metric - a good North Star usually sits upstream of revenue, tied to the value exchanged, not the money collected.

name: RICE
description: A lightweight scoring framework for prioritization questions ("how would you prioritize this backlog", "what would you build next").
example: Prompt: "You have 4 possible features and one quarter — how do you decide?" Score each on the four factors, then justify the ranking, not just the arithmetic.
steps: Reach — how many users or how much of the business this touches in a given period.
Impact — how much it moves the goal metric per user reached (often scored on a simple scale).
Confidence — how sure you are about the reach/impact estimates.
Effort — the cost to build it, usually in person-time.
Score = (Reach x Impact x Confidence) / Effort — use it to rank options, then sanity-check the ranking against judgment before presenting it.
